items.titleOriginal: Artist's Device Slows Down Citi Bikes in Less Affordable Neighborhoods
items.summaryKo: Justin Blinder's latest project examines New York City’s affordability crisis and makes the disparities felt on a physical level. This story was copublished with Next City , a nonprofit news organization reporting on solutions for more sustainable, accessible, inclusive, and equitable cities. While biking the perimeter of Prospect Park in Brooklyn, New York, on a sunny August afternoon, the pedal strokes are smooth. On the Citi Bike, I ease through all of Park Slope and most of Windsor Terrace, but as I. bike through Prospect Lefferts Gardens, also known as Flatbush, tension builds. When I enter the park at Lincoln Avenue, where Flatbush begins, there is a massive shift in my ability to move. It is jarring, and I’m forced to dismount. I’m riding around with a device attached to the e-bike that manipulates the brakes depending on the levels of rent affordability in the neighborhood you’re biking through. The device is an artwork called “ Ground Truth ,” Justin Blinder’s latest creation and part. of an exhibition with the same name. Blinder is a researcher, biker, scientist, and, at his most vivid, an artist. The exhibition explores New York City’s affordability crisis and, through the device, makes the disparities felt on a physical level. While not publicly available, he created the device for both the Lyft manual and e-bikes and has biked over 35 miles across New York City himself with it installed. Today we mourn the country singer, camp queen, hair icon, philanthropist of wide-ranging generosities, and veritable Patron Saint of the South — particularly Appalachia and. Tennessee, from which she proudly hailed and whose rich culture and people she loved deeply. In tribute to our dearest Dolly, who passed away yesterday at the age of 80, we're sharing an artwork from East Tennessee State University's 2020 exhibition dedicated to the musician. “Dolly was a proverbial ray of sunshine amidst an often dark world,” said artist Kym Day of her warm-hued portrait of the singer. “I depicted her gazing upward toward a future so bright she has to shade. her eyes from its brilliance. I wanted the painting to reflect the unwavering light that she brought to the world.” Also today, vignettes from this year's Santa Fe Indian Market, a documentary that draws on the archive of late lesbian filmmaker Barbara Hammer, and the dystopian story of a Kehinde Wiley painting removed by the US State Department (in an unoriginal twist, it was deemed too “woke.”) Participants in this year’s edition were unafraid to express themselves outside touristic expectations of “tradition,”.

items.titleOriginal: US State Department Takes Down “Woke” Kehinde Wiley Painting
items.summaryKo: “Young Artists After Siamesa 1960” (2015) was removed from the US Embassy in the Dominican Republic and could be sold. The Department of State removed Kehinde Wiley's 2015 commissioned painting from the United States embassy in the Dominican Republic this month, claiming that the artist's “violent and racist words and depictions” have no place in the foreign relations agency. In a statement shared with Hyperallergic , a spokesperson said that the department has consulted legal representatives to “ascertain whether. the art can be sold.” Leah Campos, the Trump-appointed US Ambassador to the Dominican Republic as of 2025, posted a video of the painting's removal on Instagram on August 11. The post's caption read: “In the Trump Administration and under my leadership we are turning away from globalist and woke ideologies and instead embracing American patriotism and the beauty of our great country! 🇺🇸” Wiley, known for painting Barack Obama's presidential portrait in 2018, was commissioned in 2013 by. the State Department to create “Young Artists After Siamesas 1960” for its Santo Domingo embassy. The painting depicts four individuals — two standing together as if they're about to dance, and two seated on the floor at their feet — against a floral-patterned backdrop. Wiley studied the work of Dominican artists Celeste Woss y Gil and Gilberto Hernández Ortega in preparation for the work, which he completed with the help of local art students.
